lead: In a CI engine, fuel is injected into hot compressed air, not mixed with air before compression. The mixture forms while ignition is already being prepared. The delay between the start of injection and the first pressure rise decides how much fuel collects before burning starts. That collected fuel burns fast in the premixed phase, and the rest burns as it mixes with air. These stages explain diesel noise, efficiency and load behaviour.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 CI working principle and Unit 2 injection timing and nozzles, plus the SI stage picture in 3.1 for contrast.

blocks.text: A CI engine has a heterogeneous charge. Liquid fuel, fuel vapour and air exist together in the cylinder. Fuel is injected near the end of compression into air hot enough to ignite it. Mixture formation and ignition therefore overlap: some fuel is still breaking into droplets and vapour while the first chemical reactions begin.

blocks.where: θ<sub>d</sub> is ignition delay in crank degrees (°CA); N is engine speed in rev/min; t<sub>d</sub> is delay in seconds. With t<sub>d</sub> in milliseconds: θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 N t<sub>ms</sub>. At 2000 rpm, 1 ms equals 12°CA.

blocks.text: Ignition delay (delay period) is measured from the start of injection to the first measurable pressure rise caused by combustion. It has two parts. Physical delay covers atomisation, vaporisation and mixing. Chemical delay covers pre-flame reactions that break fuel molecules into radicals. The pressure rise is small at first; the delay ends when heat release becomes visible on the pressure trace. Some syllabi call it the delay period.
The stages are a timeline, not separate boxes; they overlap. The figure uses injection at 12° before top dead centre (bTDC).

items: Ignition delay: start of injection to first pressure rise. Fuel accumulates in the chamber; heat release is small.
Premixed burn: fuel mixed during delay ignites quickly. The burning rate is high, so the pressure rises fast. This phase sets diesel knock; see 3.6.
Mixing-controlled burn: fuel burns as it mixes with hot air. The rate follows mixing, not chemical kinetics. Most heat is released here, but the pressure rise is gentler.
Late burning: remaining fuel burns late in expansion. The rate is low. It can raise exhaust temperature and smoke.

blocks.text: The first two stages are sometimes called the ignition and rapid-burning phases. The third is the main phase and controls torque. The fourth is afterburning. In a well-timed engine the main phase ends well before exhaust valve opening; a very long late phase wastes heat.
Delay changes with fuel, air and injection. A short delay gives a small premixed burn and soft combustion; a long delay gives a large premixed burn and diesel knock.

items: Cetane number: measure of ignition ease. Higher cetane number shortens delay; lower cetane lengthens it.
Air temperature and pressure: hotter, denser air shortens both physical and chemical delay. Higher compression ratio or boost raises air temperature and pressure.

Injection timing: advanced injection starts in cooler air, so delay in time can grow. Retarded injection starts nearer TDC in hotter air, so delay shortens, but too much retard raises exhaust temperature and smoke.
Injection pressure and atomisation: higher injection pressure gives finer droplets, more surface area, faster vaporisation, shorter physical delay.
Engine speed: at higher speed the same delay in milliseconds covers more crank degrees. Use the measured delay at that speed; do not scale a low-speed value.
Load: higher load usually gives a hotter charge and shorter delay. Very light load can give a longer delay because the charge is cooler.

blocks.text: A cold start is noisy for this reason: low air temperature and low speed lengthen delay, fuel accumulates, and premixed burn is strong.

figure.caption: Timeline from 12° before TDC to the end of late burning. Ignition delay covers injection to 2.4° after TDC; the next bars show premixed, mixing-controlled and late burning.

spec.aria: A timeline from 12 degrees before TDC: ignition delay ends at 2.4 degrees after TDC, premixed burn ends at 10.4 degrees, mixing-controlled burn ends at 40.4 degrees, and late burning ends at 55.4 degrees.

examples.question: Injection starts at 12° bTDC. The ignition delay is 1.2 ms at 2000 rpm. Find the delay in crank degrees and the crank angle where ignition starts. Premixed burn lasts 8°CA and mixing-controlled burn lasts 30°CA. Find the end of mixing-controlled burn. Take late burning as 15°CA and find its end.
steps: Crank angle per millisecond at 2000 rpm is 6N/1000 = 6×2000/1000 = 12°CA/ms.
Start of injection is 12° bTDC, which is −12° aTDC. Ignition starts at −12 + 14.4 = 2.4° after top dead centre (aTDC).
examples.answer: The ignition delay is 14.4°CA; ignition starts at 2.4° aTDC; premixed burn ends at 10.4° aTDC; mixing-controlled burn ends at 40.4° aTDC; late burning ends at 55.4° aTDC.
examples.check:
N = 2000
t_ms = 1.2
theta = 0.006 * N * t_ms
soi_atdc = -12.0
ign = soi_atdc + theta
prem_end = ign + 8.0
mix_end = prem_end + 30.0
late_end = mix_end + 15.0
print(f"{theta:.1f}")
print(f"{ign:.1f}")
print(f"{prem_end:.1f}")
print(f"{mix_end:.1f}")
print(f"{late_end:.1f}")

traps: Ignition delay is measured from start of injection to the first pressure rise, not from TDC and not from a spark; a CI engine has no spark.
Do not mix ms and °CA. Convert with θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 N t<sub>ms</sub>; at 2000 rpm, 1 ms is 12°CA.
Signed crank angles: mark bTDC as negative aTDC before adding the delay and stage lengths, or you will place ignition on the wrong side of TDC.
A long delay increases the premixed burn and diesel knock; it does not increase the mixing-controlled phase.
Cetane number is not octane number: high cetane shortens CI delay, high octane resists SI knock.

quiz.q: Define ignition delay in a CI engine.
quiz.a: Time from start of injection to the first measurable pressure rise due to combustion.

quiz.q: Why does a CI engine have a premixed burn phase?
quiz.a: Fuel injected during delay mixes and vaporises but does not burn at once; when ignition starts this accumulated fuel burns quickly.

quiz.q: Why does a higher cetane number shorten the delay period?
quiz.a: Cetane number measures ignition ease; higher value gives faster pre-flame reactions and earlier pressure rise.

quiz.q: Injection starts at 10° bTDC and delay is 12°CA. Find ignition crank angle.
At 1500 rpm, delay is 1.5 ms. Find delay in °CA.
A cold start at low speed gives noisy combustion. Explain using delay and premixed burn.
quiz.a: Cold air and low speed lengthen delay; more fuel accumulates; when ignition starts, premixed burn is strong, pressure rise is fast, noise and knock increase.

quiz.q: How do higher injection pressure and retarded injection timing each affect delay and the mixing-controlled phase?
quiz.a: Higher injection pressure: finer spray, faster vaporisation, shorter delay, smaller premixed burn, steadier mixing-controlled burn. Retard: injection nearer TDC in hotter air, shorter delay, but later end of combustion and higher exhaust temperature; mixing-controlled phase starts later.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern common-rail engines use pilot injection to shorten the main delay and reduce diesel noise. Multiple injection and low-temperature combustion aim to control the premixed burn, not remove it. Researchers read delay from in-cylinder pressure and heat-release traces. Search next for pilot injection, heat release rate and ignition delay correlation.
